title: Antiques Roadshow
alt: The family lore was that we've had it ever since it was ejected from a star-forming gas cloud, but it seems more likely that my great-grandparents probably just bought it while on vacation in the galactic thin disk.
transcript:
[Ponytail and Cueball are standing on opposite sides of a small table. On the table is a small stand, and floating above it is a tiny, glowing star, floating a couple of centimeters above. Ponytail is pointing to the star. At the bottom left is the logo of the US version of Antiques Roadshow: a treasure chest with the top partly open and the initials "AR" on the front. Extending from that to the right is a ribbon saying "Antiques Roadshow".]
Ponytail: Now, your grandmother said this was a relic low-mass population III star, from the first generation of stars.
Ponytail: Unfortunately, the high iron content shows that it formed much later, after several rounds of supernovas.
Ponytail: I'm afraid it's a population I star.
Cueball: Aw, darn.
Cueball: Well, it still has sentimental value.
explanation:
This comic purports to be a scene from the TV show , a  and  series in which members of the public can have s assessed and valued by experts. There are two common outcomes of the valuation: the item is a genuine antique of surprisingly high value, or the item is a modern replica and of a disappointingly low value. This comic shows the unusual scenario of Cueball having a  appraised — an item that doesn't normally get valued on the show and would not normally fit on a table of that size.

Stars are normally giant balls of stellar plasma that survive for billions of years (in this sense they would qualify as "antiques"); in typical xkcd fashion, some magical realism has made the stars tiny enough to be owned by people. After meeting the Roadshow experts, Cueball learns his star is not, as he had hoped, an old , but a more recent , as revealed by its iron content. Younger stars tend to have higher levels of iron, while older population III stars are composed almost entirely of hydrogen and helium. Cueball's comment "at least it has sentimental value" is similar to things people on the show say after learning that their "antique" is in fact a modern, low-value replica. 

In ,  groups stars into three broad categories based on their chemical composition, which is correlated with when the stars formed during the history of the universe. Population III stars, which were the first stars to form after the , have never been directly observed. It is thought that they were very large, and formed out of gas that contained no heavy elements such as iron. As they were large, they burned their fuel rapidly and exploded in , seeding the universe with the first elements heavier than hydrogen and helium. The direct observation of a population III star would be a major result in astronomy, and hence very valuable in scientific terms. A low-mass population III star in particular (as Cueball thought his star was) would be especially interesting, as these would be rarer in population III than they are in population I. In the local universe, these are the only population III stars that could be observed, as the larger ones have much shorter lifespans. Population I stars are much more common; all the stars visible in the sky, including the Sun, are population I stars. Despite being cosmologically later in evolution, these stars can be billions of years old, older than any object assessed by the Roadshow.

The title text about "family lore" echoes other things that happen in Antiques Roadshow, with people who are having items assessed often having family stories about the items. The "star-forming gas cloud" refers to clouds of gas and dust called  that are the common birthplaces of stars. Stars can get ejected from them via a gravitational slingshot from other star(s). The "" is a part of a spiral galaxy that contains most of the galaxy's stars.
